items.title: The Next Film From Disney and Pixar is a Crime Movie set in Italy… with Cats
items.summary:
Listen up, wiseguys. There’s a new Disney/Pixar movie coming out, and it’s a crime movie! Specifically, it’s a movie about the Italian mob. It takes place in Venice, Italy, and is the story of a scrawny, impoverished young fellow named Nero (voiced by Mark Ruffalo) who is taken in by a powerful crime family. In exchange for this, his job is to steal things for them… often at great personal risk.

Also, they’re all cats. Everybody’s a cat. Well, a couple of characters seem to be rodents. And there’s a pigeon, I think. But it’s mostly cats. The film is titled Gatto  (which is Italian for “cat”).

Anyway, Nero starts to find himself in very dangerous situations, working as a thief for the (literal) fat cat crime boss Rocco, and learns that he has nine lives that he’s wasting, dying while doing criminal errands. Thus, he asks himself the great questions many crime movie protagonists ask themselves: is everything he’s doing worth  it? Is he living a life that’s worth living as if it’s his only one? How can he change his life so that it’s full of meaning?

In addition to Ruffalo, the voice cast includes: Laurence Fishburne, Enrico Casarosa (who also directs), John Turturro, Isabella Rossellini, Natasia Demetriou, Jamie Demetriou, Jason Schwartzman, Saverio Raimondo, Jason Mantzoukas, Tracey Ullman, Marco Calvani, and Rhys Darby.

Perhaps it’s a great film to take your children to as you start to introduce them to the “mafia movie” genre. Watch  Gatto  and then  The Godfather  and find out which one they like better!

The film will be in theaters next March.  Ci vediamo!
items.t: The Next Film From Disney and Pixar is a Crime Movie set in Italy… with Cats

items.title: But is it a crime to fight a bear?
items.summary:
Adult, male black bears can run faster than Usain Bolt. Thirty five miles per hour. No sweat. They can sprint and jump and climb full speed up a one hundred foot tree in a matter of seconds. They can flip three hundred pound rocks with one forepaw and drag thousand pound carcasses with ease. Their muscle fibers are packed so tightly and can generate enough raw horsepower that they can tear open car doors like we’d open a refrigerator. They’re six feet tall standing on their back legs and they’ve got two inch claws built for digging and climbing or slashing. The average man would have to be insane to try and fight one in the real world. But in the world of fiction, this idea makes one hell of a fun premise to write about and during my research it brought up an interesting question: 

Fighting a bear is crazy, sure, but is it a crime? 

First, Brick Bridger, our hero in Bear Brawl , is not your average man. He’s 6’6” tall and weighs 265 pounds. He’s a two-time collegiate wrestling champion and had eight wins in the UFC before he retired. And he’s properly motivated. A rogue, 450-pound black bear killed his mom and put his brother in a wheelchair.  

The book explores what would happen if a man such as this dedicated his life to training, tracking, finding and fighting this bear with no weapons to get revenge. He enlists a zoologist, his ex-wrestling coach, local trackers and hunters and learns everything he can about this bear to prepare for the battle. 

But unlike, say, Chief Martin Brody, in Jaws , who heads out into the ocean as a law enforcement officer to hunt the…
items.t: But is it a crime to fight a bear?

items.title: The Best Psychological Thrillers of the Month: November 2026
items.summary:
In these new psychological thrillers, editors are taken hostage, cat-sitters become amateur sleuths, several small towns are ripped apart by scandal, and long-buried crimes come rising to the surface. All blurbs are my own, unless otherwise stated. Enjoy!

Stephanie Wrobel,  Revenge Plot 

(Berkley)

Wrobel’s latest is her best yet, chock-full of twists, turns, and unexpected reversals, with a perfectly constructed plot that’s also a rollicking good satire on the publishing industry. Revenge Plot certainly earns its comparisons to  Misery,  a loving homage that also manages to be entirely surprising. Here’s the gist: a desperate writer, young child in tow, shows up at a famous editor’s winter retreat and holds her hostage whilst making her read his manuscript (a fantasy shared by many writerly hopefuls, surely). As is true of all the best psychological thrillers, a series of well-paced reveals allows for constant reassessment of Wrobel’s characters and their unfortunate predicament, all leading up to the shocking denouement.

Katie Collom, Terrarium 

(Bantam)

Collom won me as a fan with her excellent tale of feminist vengeance,  Peter Miles Must Die,  and her new book seems tailor-made for this Austin-based cat-loving crime editor. In Terrarium,  a desperate barista and wannabe veterinarian finds her cat-sitting side gigs drying up after an unfortunate incident; a new job taking care of a wealthy artist’s big fluffy baby drops into her lap at the best possible time, but could her new employer be the Rainey Street killer? Fingers crossed!

May Cobb, All the Little Secrets…
items.t: The Best Psychological Thrillers of the Month: November 2026

items.title: Wendy M. Barnhart on our enduring fascination with female serial killers
items.summary:
A question was presented to me: Why do female serial killers fascinate us? I count myself in that fascination camp—my latest novel, Scaled Vengeance , focuses on a female serial killer, and I admit that the research I did for the novel enthralled me.

But is it just female serial killers who intrigue us? Or serial killers in general?

The obvious answer is that all serial killers pique our interest. The act of murdering another person is shocking. But to kill and kill and kill again is outrageous. And intense. And next-level-frightening. It’s tough to understand how one person could repeatedly want to do such a thing. Even with all of the articles written, and documentaries produced that touch on childhoods, motivations, objectives, and any other manner of revelation, I’m not sure we still “get it.” I definitely don’t.

There are some theories that, like true crime in general, audiences want to learn about serial killers so we can better understand threats. I’m not quite on board with that idea. There’s no signal in my brain telling me to be prepared should I ever encounter a serial killer, but I admit I do find them interesting nonetheless.

A little factoid to share: A friend of my mom dated Ted Bundy while he was doing his serial killer thing in Salt Lake City. She lived across the hall from him in a house that had been converted to apartments. Thankfully, she was not one of his victims, nor did he hurt her physically. (Emotionally is another thing entirely.)

But did that story give your brain a little “eek” moment? Me too. Even this many years later.

So, serial…
items.t: Wendy M. Barnhart on our enduring fascination with female serial killers

items.title: Chimera
items.summary:
Manchester, New Hampshire 1982

Rina Varger beat her palm against the old Ford pickup’s door in time to Aerosmith’s “Push Comes to Shove” as she drove across the bridge and into town. It was the morning of the tenth of September and the Merrimack was running high after a week of torrential rain, debris and dead brush from upriver borne along by the surging brown water. The wind in her face felt good after a day spent scrubbing years of dust and nameless gunk from between sticky floorboards. Everything had to be perfect for Aunt Eleanor’s wedding. Nana Marian was losing her mind trying to get the house in shape, running their skinless maid Kate Bartlett ragged.

A little after eight Rina parked in front of Julian and Eddie’s place, a cramped two-story bungalow with a patchy lawn and huge stands of sumac nearly obscuring its front entrance and encroaching on its drive-way. Julian, an aging queen cast off by a prominent Cape Cod family, owned Plover Antiques downtown. Eddie Means was a veterinarian at the Franklin Park Zoo in Boston, and had been the Varger family’s meat man for almost ten years. Rina killed the engine and stepped out onto the curb, fishing in her jacket pockets for her cigarettes. She was about to light up when she heard voices coming from the direction of the driveway. She pocketed her smokes and went around the house, moving slowly, keeping to the shadows of the sumac stand.

Four teenage boys, maybe fifteen or sixteen, and a girl who looked a little younger stood in a half circle at the end of the driveway, in front of Julian’s garage. Another girl, maybe…
items.t: Chimera

items.title: The Giggler: The forgotten serial killer who haunted Boston’s South Station
items.summary:
Boston’s South Station was less than 70 years old in 1969 but seemed much older. It certainly lacked the glamour of nearby North Station, home to the Boston Garden, where the city’s basketball and hockey teams played and where the Rolling Stones and James Brown performed for screaming teenagers. In comparison, the South Station stop on 700 Atlantic Avenue was a dreary place for tired daily commuters on their way to the suburbs of the South Shore. With its high-domed ceiling and rickety escalators built during the Depression era, South Station managed to be both enormous and decrepit, a sickly old giant in need of urgent care. As the Boston Globe said a few years later, the once thriving railroad stop was “now staggering along in the last stages of neglect.” 

Yet even as it faced the threat of the wrecking ball, the station remained busy, particularly at holiday time. On Friday, December 26, a 9-year-old Dorchester boy named Kenny Martin wandered into the station with a friend, Thomas Lydon. It was the day after Christmas and Kenny, who had come into Downtown Boston to buy some Boy Scout equipment, spent the afternoon horsing around with Lydon at the station. They’d chased each other up and down the escalators, running through the crowd of postholiday shoppers. As the afternoon came to an end, Lydon departed, while Kenny planned to take the train back home. 

In his brown-checked jacket with fur collar, blue bell-bottom pants, and orange work boots, Kenny was a typical Dorchester boy, coming home from a day of fun. He was the youngest of four children, small for his age at…
items.t: The Giggler: The forgotten serial killer who haunted Boston’s South Station

items.title: Snowbound suspense: 5 thrillers set during snowstorms
items.summary:
A glorious snowfall can conjure up warm thoughts of hot cocoa, kids tossing snowballs and building forts, the holidays, a still, peaceful white landscape. But it can also create a darker, dangerous flipside. Getting trapped, losing power, being exposed to the elements. I’ve always loved thrillers that take advantage of a bad snowstorm–of bringing cold, heartless motivations to frozen landscapes.

In my latest novel, The Cold Read , I take full advantage of the chilling nature of a snowy locale by setting my book at a remote, abandoned ski resort, where the elements quickly take on a very sinister nature.

Here are a few other books that do the same. If you want to shiver your way through a good mystery without actually having to worry about frostbite, you’ll want to pick up these other snowbound stories as we head into the winter season.

*

Ruth Ware, One by One 

This novel, involving a group of co-workers setting off on a retreat, would be a nightmare on its own even without the thriller elements. Traveling with coworkers! Skits! Presentations! The terror! To make things much, much worse, however, this work retreat involves an avalanche, power loss, and the little matter of the group disappearing and dying off.

The characters make this book the tense, twisty thriller it is. It’s an enjoyable puzzle to piece together as you read.

Allie Reynolds, Shiver 

A group of competitive snowboarding friends reunite in the French alps at the ski resort where their frenemy mysteriously disappeared some years before. But weird things immediately start to happen. Their cell phones…
items.t: Snowbound suspense: 5 thrillers set during snowstorms

items.title: Deep cuts: The vampire stories that inspired Caitlin Starling’s new novel, ‘Milkteeth’
items.summary:
You’ve watched or read (or both!) Interview with the Vampire , Dracula , Sinners , and all the other heavy-hitters, you’ve dabbled in playing Vampire: The Masquerade… now what?

You could always check out Milkteeth , my newest novel, which asks the burning question: what if vampires had to breastfeed?

…I promise it makes more sense in context.

More seriously, it’s about Beatrice, a vampiric broodmother; she raises the fledgling children of other vampires through the first three years of their transformation, until they are both mentally mature and able to consume human blood safely. Beatrice is very good at what she does, but she’s looked down on with a certain amount of disgust by the vampires who rely on her.

When she takes on a challenging new charge and her body begins to change in inexplicable ways, she has to figure out a solution before everything can be taken for her—or worse, she devours her own brood.

It’s equal parts domestic and rancid, filthy and tender, violent and intimate. And if that’s less your speed, or you want to see some of the works that are responsible, at least in part, for Milkteeth’s existence, here are some lesser-known vampire stories that I’ve enjoyed.

*

TV Show 

Penny Dreadful 

If you’ve heard of anything on this list, I’d wager it’s this show. Running three seasons on Showtime, Penny Dreadful brought together a broad variety of Victorian pulp horror into an atmospheric, brutal, and occasionally messy symphony. While there are a lot of moving parts, Eva Green’s character, Vanessa Ives, finds herself embroiled on a take on Dracula that…

items.title: Katie Collom on exploring her relationship with true crime in a suspense novel
items.summary:
True crime and I go way back.

My first encounter with the genre was during an annual trip to visit my grandma. Each year, I’d dive into the pile of Reader’s Digest she’d acquired, devouring them cover to cover. It was in one these that I read an article about a criminal profiler who suffered a mental breakdown.

This left a deep impression on my eleven-year-old mind. I couldn’t believe there were human beings who could commit acts so horrific, they actually drove their pursuers insane. More importantly, there were people whose jobs were to figure out how sociopaths think!

I was hooked.

I continued to seek out more content about criminals and their crimes. The effect could be…less than healthy. I recall spending a night at a friend’s house and being unable to sleep because it was located somewhat near a railroad track. Just the week before, I’d watched a show about a killer who chose his victims by their proximity to the trains he freight-hopped.

Later as a teenager, my worries became more specific: I’d fret daily about my parents properly locking the windows and doors in our home before we all went to bed. Thankfully we didn’t have a basement or an attic because if we did, I probably wouldn’t have ever gotten a solid night’s sleep.

It wasn’t until I was an adult that these types of articles and shows were given a label. By then, true-crime podcasts and TV series had become so trendy they were their own genre. The sudden abundance of content seemed tailor-made for someone like me: a person who’d been consuming these stories steadily from childhood. Even better, there…
items.t: Katie Collom on exploring her relationship with true crime in a suspense novel

items.title: Jacob Elordi will star in an adaptation of The Executioner’s Song
items.summary:
Fresh off his Oscar-nominated turn as the Creature in Frankenstein,  Jacob Elordi is set to star in and produce an adaptation of Norman Mailer’s Pulitzer prize-winning 1979 novel The Executioner’s Song .

The Executioner’s Song is a complex, fictionalizd biography-of-sorts of American murderer Gary Gilmore, who, after being convicted of murdering two men in Utah, insisted on his death penalty sentence being carried out, despite the national moratorium on capital punishment implemented by the Supreme Court case Furman v. Georgia , which decided that different states’ inconsistent approaches toward criminal execution violated the Eight and Fourteenth amendments. Gilmore, who fought anti-capital punishment attorneys insistent on preserving his life, was eventually executed by firing squad in 1977.

The novel is broken up into two sections: “Western Voices,” and “Eastern Voices.” The first part is about the forces that made Gilmore into the man he became (including a youth spent in child detention facilities in the barren American west), while the second is about the media frenzy and national debate around the case, and spotlights, in particular, Gilmore’s relationship with the celebrity photographer Lawrence “Larry” Schiller, who conducted many interviews with Gilmore, his family, and others related to the case and brought the project to Mailer, in the first place.

Mailer continued Schiller’s research to craft a nearly 1000-page, plainly-written epic about the nihilism of the American West, the American proclivity towards violence, media madness, the exploitation of the…
items.t: Jacob Elordi will star in an adaptation of The Executioner’s Song

“I’d feel that guilty about it. I’d pass them notes, saying I’m so sorry about this,” he said. “But in the end, I was just that numb to it, and fearless as well. I’d walk in with a suitcase and ram everything into it, and not think twice about it.”
